claim: Connections from the ventral hippocampus (vHPC) to the prefrontal cortex (PFC) regulate cognition, emotion, and memory.
source: Connections from the ventral hippocampus (vHPC) to the prefrontal cortex (PFC) regulate cognition, emotion, and memory.
evidence: This is a general statement about the functional role of vHPC-PFC connections, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Disruption of inhibitory networks in the PFC is thought to contribute to mental health disorders.
source: These functions are also tightly controlled by inhibitory networks in the PFC, whose disruption is thought to contribute to mental health disorders.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific understanding about the role of PFC inhibitory networks in mental health.

claim: Cholecystokinin (CCK+), parvalbumin (PV+), and somatostatin (SOM+) expressing interneurons are prominent in layer 5 (L5) of infralimbic PFC.
source: We first show that cholecystokinin (CCK+), parvalbumin (PV+), and somatostatin (SOM+) expressing interneurons are prominent in layer 5 (L5) of infralimbic PFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations using transgenic mice and viral labeling approaches described in the manuscript.

claim: vHPC inputs primarily activate CCK+ and PV+ interneurons, with weaker connections onto SOM+ interneurons.
source: We then show that vHPC inputs primarily activate CCK+ and PV+ interneurons, with weaker connections onto SOM+ interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings and optogenetic stimulation experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: CCK+ interneurons make stronger synapses onto pyramidal tract (PT) cells over nearby intratelencephalic (IT) cells.
source: CCK+ interneurons make stronger synapses onto pyramidal tract (PT) cells over nearby intratelencephalic (IT) cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by paired recordings from IT and PT cells shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CCK+ inputs undergo depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition (DSI) and CB1 receptor modulation only at IT cells.
source: However, CCK+ inputs undergo depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition (DSI) and CB1 receptor modulation only at IT cells.
evidence: This is supported by DSI experiments and pharmacological manipulations shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: vHPC-evoked feed-forward inhibition undergoes DSI only at IT cells.
source: Moreover, vHPC-evoked feed-forward inhibition undergoes DSI only at IT cells, confirming a central role for CCK+ interneurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 7 where vHPC inputs were stimulated and DSI was measured at IT and PT cells.

claim: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) controls cognitive and emotional behaviors.
source: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) controls cognitive and emotional behaviors (Euston et al., 2012; Miller and Cohen, 2001) and is disrupted in many neuropsychiatric disorders (Godsil et al., 2013; Sigurdsson and Duvarci, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The PFC is disrupted in many neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) controls cognitive and emotional behaviors (Euston et al., 2012; Miller and Cohen, 2001) and is disrupted in many neuropsychiatric disorders (Godsil et al., 2013; Sigurdsson and Duvarci, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Strong, unidirectional connections from the ventral hippocampus (vHPC) contribute to both working memory and threat conditioning in rodents.
source: Strong, unidirectional connections from the ventral hippocampus (vHPC) contribute to both working memory and threat conditioning in rodents (Jones and Wilson, 2005; Sotres-Bayon et al., 2012; Spellman et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dysfunction of vHPC to PFC connectivity is implicated in schizophrenia, anxiety disorders, chronic stress disorders, and depression.
source: Dysfunction of vHPC to PFC connectivity is also implicated in schizophrenia, anxiety disorders, chronic stress disorders, and depression (Godsil et al., 2013; Sigurdsson and Duvarci, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The vHPC primarily projects to the ventral medial PFC in rodents, with axons most prominent in layer 5 (L5) of infralimbic (IL) PFC.
source: The vHPC primarily projects to the ventral medial PFC in rodents, with axons most prominent in layer 5 (L5) of infralimbic (IL) PFC (Phillips et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: vHPC excitatory inputs are much stronger at intratelencephalic (IT) cells than nearby pyramidal tract (PT) cells.
source: These excitatory inputs contact multiple populations of pyramidal cells and are much stronger at intratelencephalic (IT) cells than nearby pyramidal tract (PT) cells (Liu and Carter, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: vHPC inputs can drive the robust firing of IT cells.
source: vHPC inputs can drive the robust firing of IT cells (Liu and Carter, 2018), which may be important for maintaining activity during behavioral tasks (Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016; Spellman et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: vHPC inputs evoke prominent feed-forward inhibition at pyramidal cells.
source: However, they also evoke prominent feed-forward inhibition at pyramidal cells (Marek et al., 2018), and excitation and inhibition evolve with different dynamics (Liu and Carter, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) interneurons mediate feed-forward inhibition via strong synapses at the soma of pyramidal cells.
source: Parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) interneurons mediate feed-forward inhibition via strong synapses at the soma of pyramidal cells (Atallah et al., 2012; Cruikshank et al., 2007; Gabernet et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing (SOM+) interneurons mediate feed-back inhibition via facilitating synapses onto the dendrites.
source: By contrast, somatostatin-expressing (SOM+) interneurons mediate feed-back inhibition via facilitating synapses onto the dendrites (Gentet et al., 2012; Silberberg and Markram, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During trains of repetitive activity, SOM+ interneurons can also participate in feed-forward inhibition.
source: However, during trains of repetitive activity, SOM+ interneurons can also participate in feed-forward inhibition (McGarry and Carter, 2016; Tan et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Recent in vivo studies suggest both PV+ and SOM+ interneurons may contribute to vHPC-evoked inhibition in the PFC.
source: Interestingly, recent in vivo studies suggest both PV+ and SOM+ interneurons may contribute to vHPC-evoked inhibition in the PFC (Abbas et al., 2018; Marek et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is an unusually high density of cholecystokinin-expressing (CCK+) interneurons in the PFC.
source: While PV+ and SOM+ interneurons are prominent in the PFC, there is also an unusually high density of cholecystokinin-expressing (CCK+) interneurons (Whissell et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the hippocampus, CCK+ inhibitory cells help regulate the motivation and emotional state of animals.
source: In the hippocampus, these inhibitory cells help regulate the motivation and emotional state of animals (Armstrong and Soltesz, 2012; Freund, 2003; Freund and Katona, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CCK+ interneurons highly express cannabinoid type 1 (CB1) receptors on their axon terminals.
source: They also highly express cannabinoid type 1 (CB1) receptors on their axon terminals (Katona et al., 1999), and can be strongly modulated by endocannabinoids (Wilson et al., 2001; Wilson and Nicoll, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CCK+ interneurons can be strongly modulated by endocannabinoids.
source: They also highly express cannabinoid type 1 (CB1) receptors on their axon terminals (Katona et al., 1999), and can be strongly modulated by endocannabinoids (Wilson et al., 2001; Wilson and Nicoll, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Brief depolarization of postsynaptic pyramidal cells releases endocannabinoids that bind to CB1 receptors on CCK+ axon terminals and inhibit presynaptic GABA release, a process known as depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition (DSI).
source: For example, brief depolarization of postsynaptic pyramidal cells releases endocannabinoids that bind to CB1 receptors on CCK+ axon terminals and inhibit presynaptic GABA release, a process known as depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition (DSI) (Wilson and Nicoll, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CCK is expressed at low levels in pyramidal cells, which makes CCK+ interneurons challenging to specifically target.
source: A major technical reason is the low-level expression of CCK in pyramidal cells (Taniguchi et al., 2011), which makes CCK+ interneurons challenging to specifically target.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Expressing Cre-dependent reporters in CCK-Cre transgenics also labels pyramidal cells in the cortex.
source: For example, expressing Cre-dependent reporters in CCK-Cre transgenics also label pyramidal cells in the cortex (Taniguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Intersectional viruses using the Dlx enhancer can restrict expression to interneurons, overcoming the challenge of labeling CCK+ interneurons.
source: Fortunately, this challenge can be overcome with intersectional viruses using the Dlx enhancer, which restricts expression to interneurons (Dimidschstein et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: vHPC inputs evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) at −65 mV and inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) at +15 mV in IT cells.
source: Trains of vHPC inputs evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) at −65 mV and inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) at +15 mV (Figure 1C; EPSC1 = 386 ± 49 pA, IPSC1 = 961 ± 207 pA, E/I = 0.50 ± 0.08; n = 7 cells, three animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The excitation/inhibition (E/I) ratio at IT cells in response to vHPC inputs is 0.50 ± 0.08.
source: Trains of vHPC inputs evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) at −65 mV and inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) at +15 mV (Figure 1C; EPSC1 = 386 ± 49 pA, IPSC1 = 961 ± 207 pA, E/I = 0.50 ± 0.08; n = 7 cells, three animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: vHPC inputs drive robust feed-forward inhibition in deep layers of the IL PFC.
source: These findings indicate that vHPC inputs drive robust feed-forward inhibition in deep layers of the IL PFC, motivating us to identify which interneurons are responsible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data showing prominent IPSCs.

claim: Injecting AAV-DIO-GFP into CCK-Cre mice labels both CCK+ interneurons and pyramidal neurons across multiple layers.
source: To label these cells, we initially injected AAV-DIO-GFP into CCK-Cre mice but observed labeling of both interneurons and pyramidal neurons across multiple layers (Figure 1E).
evidence: This observation is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Injecting AAV-Dlx-Flex-GFP selectively labels CCK+ interneurons in the IL PFC.
source: Injecting AAV-Dlx-Flex-GFP selectively labeled CCK+ interneurons in the IL PFC, including prominent labeling in L5 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This observation is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There is little co-labeling of CCK+ cells with PV (11.3% overlap).
source: Importantly, we found little co-labeling of CCK+ cells with either PV (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; 11.3% overlap, n = 308 cells total, 17 slices, 6 animals) or SOM (6.6% overlap, n = 105 cells total, 8 slices, 3 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: There is little co-labeling of CCK+ cells with SOM (6.6% overlap).
source: Importantly, we found little co-labeling of CCK+ cells with either PV (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; 11.3% overlap, n = 308 cells total, 17 slices, 6 animals) or SOM (6.6% overlap, n = 105 cells total, 8 slices, 3 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: CCK+ interneurons have intrinsic properties with Rin = 130 ± 13 MΩ, Vm = −68 ± 1 mV, Sag = 4.1 ± 1.0%, Adaptation = 0.81 ± 0.04, Tau = 9.1 ± 0.6 ms.
source: We found both axons and dendrites in L5 of IL PFC, and intrinsic properties similar to reports in other parts of the brain (Figure 1H; Rin = 130 ± 13 MΩ, Vm = −68 ± 1 mV, Sag = 4.1 ± 1.0%, Adaptation = 0.81 ± 0.04, Tau = 9.1 ± 0.6 ms; n = 12 cells, 4 animals) (Daw et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1H.

claim: vHPC inputs evoke robust EPSCs at CCK+ interneurons, which are similar in amplitude to IT cells (CCK+/IT ratio = 0.56).
source: We found that vHPC inputs evoked robust EPSCs at CCK+ interneurons, which were similar in amplitude to IT cells (Figure 2A; IT = 674 ± 102 pA, CCK+ = 413 ± 89 pA, CCK+/IT ratio = 0.56, p = 0.13; n = 9 pairs, 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2A.

claim: vHPC inputs evoke prominent EPSCs at PV+ interneurons, with comparable amplitudes at IT cells (PV+/IT ratio = 0.94).
source: We also found prominent vHPC-evoked EPSCs at PV+ interneurons, with comparable amplitudes at IT cells (Figure 2B; IT = 569 ± 91 pA, PV+ = 555 ± 83 pA, PV+/IT ratio = 0.94, p = 0.82; n = 9 pairs, 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2B.

claim: vHPC inputs evoke much smaller EPSCs at SOM+ interneurons compared to IT cells (SOM+/IT ratio = 0.17).
source: By contrast, vHPC inputs evoked much smaller EPSCs at SOM+ interneurons compared to IT cells (Figure 2C; IT = 421 ± 69 pA, SOM+ = 95 ± 33 pA, SOM+/IT ratio = 0.17, p = 0.004; n = 9 pairs, 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All three cell types (CCK+, PV+, SOM+) receive direct vHPC inputs, with greater responses at CCK+ and PV+ interneurons.
source: These findings show that all three cell types receive direct vHPC inputs, with greater responses at CCK+ and PV+ interneurons.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the electrophysiological data from Figure 2A-C.

claim: Single vHPC inputs evoke APs in pairs of CCK+ and IT cells but the interneurons show a higher probability of firing (IT = 0.32 ± 0.15, CCK+ = 0.84 ± 0.11, p = 0.03).
source: We found that single vHPC inputs evoked APs in pairs of CCK+ and IT cells but the interneurons showed a higher probability of firing (Figure 2D; AP probability: IT = 0.32 ± 0.15, CCK+ = 0.84 ± 0.11, p = 0.03; n = 9 pairs, 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 2D.

claim: vHPC inputs preferentially activate PV+ over IT cells (IT = 0.06 ± 0.06, PV+ = 0.65 ± 0.17, p = 0.04).
source: Similarly, we observed that vHPC inputs also preferentially activate PV+ over IT cells (Figure 2E; AP probability: IT = 0.06 ± 0.06, PV+ = 0.65 ± 0.17, p = 0.04; n = 8 pairs, 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SOM+ interneurons remain unresponsive to vHPC inputs, even when using higher light intensities that activate IT cells (IT = 0.81 ± 0.12, SOM+ = 0.13 ± 0.06, p = 0.01).
source: By contrast, SOM+ interneurons remained unresponsive to vHPC inputs, even when using higher light intensities that were able to activate IT cells (Figure 2F; AP probability: IT = 0.81 ± 0.12, SOM+ = 0.13 ± 0.06, p = 0.01; n = 7 pairs, 3 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CCK+ and PV+ interneurons are engaged by vHPC inputs and mediate feed-forward inhibition.
source: These results established a hierarchy for activation, suggesting CCK+ and PV+ interneurons are engaged by vHPC inputs and mediate feed-forward inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the action potential probability data from Figure 2.

claim: EPSCs at CCK+ interneurons strongly depress over the course of stimulus trains (EPSC2 / EPSC1: CCK+ = 0.82 ± 0.06).
source: We observed that EPSCs at CCK+ and PV+ interneurons strongly depress over the course of stimulus trains (Figure 3A & B; EPSC2 / EPSC1: CCK+ = 0.82 ± 0.06; n = 6 cells, 3 animals; PV+ = 0.88 ± 0.06; n = 7 cells, 3 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings during repetitive stimulation shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: EPSCs at PV+ interneurons strongly depress over the course of stimulus trains (EPSC2 / EPSC1: PV+ = 0.88 ± 0.06).
source: We observed that EPSCs at CCK+ and PV+ interneurons strongly depress over the course of stimulus trains (Figure 3A & B; EPSC2 / EPSC1: CCK+ = 0.82 ± 0.06; n = 6 cells, 3 animals; PV+ = 0.88 ± 0.06; n = 7 cells, 3 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings during repetitive stimulation shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: EPSCs at SOM+ interneurons initially facilitate during trains (EPSC2 / EPSC1 = 1.78 ± 0.23).
source: By contrast, the EPSCs at SOM+ interneurons initially facilitated during trains (Figure 3A & B; EPSC2 / EPSC1 = 1.78 ± 0.23; n = 8 cells, 3 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings during repetitive stimulation shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: vHPC engages all three cell types, with connections at PV+ and CCK+ interneurons strong but depressing, and those at SOM+ interneurons weak but facilitating.
source: These results indicate that vHPC engages all three cell types, with connections at PV+ and CCK+ interneurons strong but depressing, and those at SOM+ interneurons weak but facilitating.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the short-term plasticity data from Figure 3.

claim: Stimulus trains of vHPC inputs generate decreasing AP probabilities at CCK+ interneurons (stimulus 1 and 2 AP probabilities: CCK+ = 0.97 ± 0.02 and 0.75 ± 0.06).
source: We observed that stimulus trains of vHPC inputs generated decreasing AP probabilities at CCK+ and PV+ interneurons (Figure 3C & D; stimulus 1 and 2 AP probabilities: CCK+ = 0.97 ± 0.02 and 0.75 ± 0.06; n = 12 cells, 5 animals; PV+ = 0.96 ± 0.02 and 0.70 ± 0.13; n = 6 cells, 3 animals;).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp recordings during repetitive stimulation shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Stimulus trains of vHPC inputs generate decreasing AP probabilities at PV+ interneurons (stimulus 1 and 2 AP probabilities: PV+ = 0.96 ± 0.02 and 0.70 ± 0.13).
source: We observed that stimulus trains of vHPC inputs generated decreasing AP probabilities at CCK+ and PV+ interneurons (Figure 3C & D; stimulus 1 and 2 AP probabilities: CCK+ = 0.97 ± 0.02 and 0.75 ± 0.06; n = 12 cells, 5 animals; PV+ = 0.96 ± 0.02 and 0.70 ± 0.13; n = 6 cells, 3 animals;).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp recordings during repetitive stimulation shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: SOM+ interneurons do not fire with single pulses of vHPC inputs but are activated during trains (stimulus 1 and 2 AP probabilities: IT = 0 and 0, SOM+ = 0 and 0.57 ± 0.14).
source: By contrast, although SOM+ interneurons did not fire with single pulses of vHPC inputs, they were activated during trains. Importantly, these responses were not due to recurrent network activity, as stimulation intensity was chosen here to ensure that IT cells remained quiescent (Figure 3C & D; stimulus 1 and 2 AP probabilities: IT = 0 and 0, SOM+ = 0 and 0.57 ± 0.14; n = 6 pairs, 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp recordings during repetitive stimulation shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: vHPC differentially engages three interneuron types with distinct dynamics during repetitive activity, with strong and depressing PV+ and CCK+ activity contributing early, and weaker but facilitating SOM+ activity contributing later.
source: These findings suggest that vHPC differentially engages three interneuron types with distinct dynamics during repetitive activity, with strong and depressing PV+ and CCK+ activity contributing early, and weaker but facilitating SOM+ activity contributing later.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data from Figure 3.

claim: Labeled CCK+ cells can be rapidly and reliably activated by brief pulses of blue light, with a single AP elicited for each pulse during the train.
source: Whole-cell current-clamp recordings showed that labeled cells could be rapidly and reliably activated by brief pulses of blue light, with a single AP elicited for each pulse during the train (Figure 4A; stimulus 1 to 5, AP number: 1.0 ± 0.0, n = 6 cells, 3 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CCK+-evoked IPSCs are unaffected by blockers of AMPAR (10 µM NBQX) and NMDAR (10 µM CPP) but abolished by blockers of GABAAR (10 µM gabazine).
source: We observed robust CCK+-evoked IPSCs, which were unaffected by blockers of AMPAR (10 µM NBQX) and NMDAR (10 µM CPP) but abolished by blockers of GABAAR (10 µM gabazine) (Figure 4B; ACSF = 97 ± 21 pA, NBQX+CPP = 97 ± 21 pA, gabazine = 0.4 ± 0.2 pA; ACSF versus NBQX + CPP, p = 0.69; NBQX + CPP versus gabazine, p = 0.01; n = 7 cells, 3 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CCK+ interneurons make inhibitory connections onto neighboring L5 pyramidal cells.
source: These findings indicate that CCK+ interneurons make inhibitory connections onto neighboring L5 pyramidal cells and that our viral strategy avoids contamination from excitatory contacts due to inadvertent activation of CCK+ pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pharmacological data from Figure 4B.

claim: CCK-evoked IPSCs are larger onto PT cells than IT cells (IPSC IT = 113 ± 59 pA, PT = 245 ± 79 pA, p = 0.01).
source: Recording from pairs of pyramidal cells, we found that CCK-evoked IPSCs were larger onto PT cells than IT cells (Figure 4D; IPSC IT = 113 ± 59 pA, PT = 245 ± 79 pA, p = 0.01; n = 7 pairs, 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CCK+ interneurons make cell-type specific connections, preferentially targeting PT cells in L5 of the IL PFC.
source: These findings indicate that CCK+ interneurons make cell-type specific connections, preferentially targeting PT cells in L5 of the IL PFC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the paired recording data from Figure 4D.

claim: CCK+ inputs are highly restricted to the somatic compartment of both IT and PT cells.
source: We found CCK+ inputs are highly restricted to the somatic compartment of both IT and PT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B & D).
evidence: This claim is supported by subcellular channelrhodopsin assisted circuit mapping (sCRACM) data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CCK+ inputs are primarily near the soma of IT and PT cells, in contrast to the strong dendritic innervation by SOM+, 5HT3aR+, and NDNF+ cells.
source: Therefore, in contrast to the strong dendritic innervation by SOM+, 5HT3aR+, and NDNF+ cells (Anastasiades et al., 2020; Marlin and Carter, 2014), these results indicate that CCK+ inputs are primarily near the soma of IT and PT cells.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature, supported by the sCRACM data.

claim: CB1R+ puncta show higher co-localization with CCK+ axons than with PV+ axons (puncta density in 103/µm2: PV+CB1R+ = 3.79 ± 0.64, GFP+CB1R+ = 11.27 ± 1.5, p=0.0003).
source: We found CB1R+ puncta showed higher co-localization with CCK+ axons (based on GFP+ expression) than with PV+ axons (Figure 4E–G; puncta density in 103/µm2: PV+CB1R+ = 3.79 ± 0.64, GFP+CB1R+ = 11.27 ± 1.5, p=0.0003).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: CCK+ interneurons are enriched with presynaptic CB1Rs and are likely to undergo endocannabinoid modulation.
source: These results suggest that CCK+ interneurons are enriched with presynaptic CB1Rs and are likely to undergo endocannabinoid modulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunocytochemistry data from Figure 4E-G.

claim: CB1R+ puncta density is much greater at IT cells than PT cells (IT = 9.3 ± 0.5 puncta/cell, PT = 5.7 ± 0.5 puncta/cell, p<0.0001).
source: While we observed CB1R+ puncta around the cell bodies of both cell types (Figure 4I), their density was much greater at IT cells (Figure 4J; IT = 9.3 ± 0.5 puncta/cell, PT = 5.7 ± 0.5 puncta/cell, p<0.0001; n = 4 animals, 247 IT cells, 207 PT cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4I-J.

claim: Presynaptic CB1Rs are more prominent at perisomatic connections onto IT cells, suggesting that endocannabinoid modulation may be more extensive at those projection neurons.
source: These results indicate that presynaptic CB1Rs are more prominent at perisomatic connections onto IT cells, suggesting that endocannabinoid modulation may be more extensive at those projection neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunocytochemistry data from Figure 4I-J.

claim: CCK+-evoked IPSCs at IT cells undergo pronounced DSI that recovers to baseline when inputs are stimulated again 30 s later (IPSC1: before = 158 ± 34 pA, after = 91 ± 24 pA, recovery = 149 ± 33 pA; DSI ratio = 0.57 ± 0.06, p = 0.004).
source: In voltage-clamp recordings from retrogradely labeled IT cells, we found that CCK+-evoked IPSCs underwent pronounced DSI that recovered to baseline when inputs were stimulated again 30 s later (Figure 5C & F; IPSC1: before = 158 ± 34 pA, after = 91 ± 24 pA, recovery = 149 ± 33 pA; DSI ratio = 0.57 ± 0.06, p = 0.004; n = 9 cells, 5 animals), with these recovery kinetics similar to previous reports in other preparations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; n = 10 cells, four animals) (Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by DSI experiments shown in Figure 5C and F.

claim: The CB1R inverse agonist 10 µM AM-251 blocks DSI at IT cells (IPSC1: before = 189 ± 53 pA, after = 168 ± 44 pA, recovery = 185 ± 55; DSI ratio = 0.92 ± 0.04, p = 0.08).
source: We confirmed the involvement of endocannabinoid signaling by blocking DSI with the CB1R inverse agonist 10 µM AM-251 (Figure 5D & F; IPSC1: before = 189 ± 53 pA, after = 168 ± 44 pA, recovery = 185 ± 55; DSI ratio = 0.92 ± 0.04, p = 0.08; n = 7 cells, 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5D and F.

claim: PV+ and SOM+-evoked IPSCs at IT cells have minimal DSI (IPSC1 DSI ratio: PV+ = 0.94 ± 0.02, p = 0.11; SOM+ = 0.87 ± 0.05, p = 0.02).
source: We also confirmed this modulation was specific to CCK+ inputs, as PV+ and SOM+-evoked IPSCs at IT cells had minimal DSI (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2; IPSC1 DSI ratio: PV+ = 0.94 ± 0.02, p = 0.11; n = 7 cells, 3 animals; SOM+ = 0.87 ± 0.05, p = 0.02; n = 8 cells, 3 animals; PV+ versus CCK+, p = 0.0007; SOM+ versus CCK+, p = 0.008).
evidence: This claim is supported by DSI experiments shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is minimal DSI at PT cells (IPSC1before = 208 ± 40 pA, after = 202 ± 44 pA, recovery = 205 ± 40 pA; DSI ratio = 0.95 ± 0.04, p = 0.22).
source: Surprisingly, we found minimal DSI at PT cells, indicating modulation also strongly depends on postsynaptic cell type (Figure 5E & F; IPSC1before = 208 ± 40 pA, after = 202 ± 44 pA, recovery = 205 ± 40 pA; DSI ratio = 0.95 ± 0.04, p = 0.22; n = 7 cells, 3 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by DSI experiments shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Although CCK+ interneurons broadly contact L5 pyramidal cells, the connections undergo prominent CB1R-mediated DSI only at IT cells and not nearby PT cells.
source: These findings indicate that although CCK+ interneurons broadly contact L5 pyramidal cells, the connections undergo prominent CB1R-mediated DSI only at IT cells and not nearby PT cells.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the DSI data from Figure 5.

claim: Equivalent CB1R modulation of CCK+ inputs to IT cells also occurs under more physiological conditions.
source: Together, these experiments indicate that equivalent CB1R modulation of CCK+ inputs to IT cells also occurs under more physiological conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on current-clamp DSI experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: WIN reduces CCK+-evoked IPSCs at IT cells, which is reversed by AM-251 (baseline = 234 ± 53 pA, WIN = 106 ± 26 pA, AM-251 = 206 ± 50 pA; baseline versus WIN, p = 0.008; WIN versus AM-251, p = 0.016).
source: In voltage-clamp recordings from L5 IT cells, we found that WIN reduced CCK+-evoked IPSCs, which was reversed by AM-251 (Figure 6A & C; baseline = 234 ± 53 pA, WIN = 106 ± 26 pA, AM-251 = 206 ± 50 pA; baseline versus WIN, p = 0.008; WIN versus AM-251, p = 0.016; n = 8 cells, 5 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: Washing in AM-251 alone slightly increases CCK+ inputs at IT cells, confirming weak tonic CB1R activation (baseline = 186.7 ± 32 pA, AM-251 = 204.1 ± 29 pA, AM-251/baseline = 1.18 ± 0.10, p = 0.01).
source: Recording at IT cells, we found that washing in AM-251 alone slightly increased the CCK+ inputs, confirming weak tonic CB1R activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; baseline = 186.7 ± 32 pA, AM-251 = 204.1 ± 29 pA, AM-251/baseline = 1.18 ± 0.10, p = 0.01, n = 8 cells, 5 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither WIN nor AM-251 have any effect on CCK+-evoked IPSCs at PT cells (baseline = 292 ± 55 pA, WIN = 250 ± 36 pA, AM-251 = 281 ± 37 pA; baseline versus. WIN, p = 0.81; WIN versus AM-251, p = 0.22).
source: By contrast, recordings at PT cells, we found that neither WIN nor AM-251 had any effect on CCK+-evoked IPSCs, consistent with a lack of DSI (Figure 6B & C; baseline = 292 ± 55 pA, WIN = 250 ± 36 pA, AM-251 = 281 ± 37 pA; baseline versus. WIN, p = 0.81; WIN versus AM-251, p = 0.22; n = 7 cells, 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The activation of CB1 receptors strongly reduces CCK+-evoked IPSCs only at IT cells but not neighboring PT cells (WIN/baseline: IT = 0.44 ± 0.05, PT = 0.92 ± 0.09, p = 0.001).
source: Overall, the activation of CB1 receptors strongly reduced CCK+-evoked IPSCs only at IT cells but not neighboring PT cells (Figure 6C; WIN/baseline: IT = 0.44 ± 0.05, PT = 0.92 ± 0.09, p = 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Wash-in of WIN increases the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) at IT cells, suggesting presynaptic modulation of release probability by CB1Rs (IPSC2 / IPSC1: baseline = 0.48 ± 0.03, WIN = 0.59 ± 0.03, AM-251 = 0.54 ± 0.02; baseline versus WIN, p = 0.03; WIN versus AM-251, p = 0.22).
source: Interestingly, during trains of CCK+ stimulation, wash-in of WIN also increased the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) at IT cells, suggesting presynaptic modulation of release probability by CB1Rs (Figure 6D; IPSC2 / IPSC1: baseline = 0.48 ± 0.03, WIN = 0.59 ± 0.03, AM-251 = 0.54 ± 0.02; baseline versus WIN, p = 0.03; WIN versus AM-251, p = 0.22; n = 7 cells, 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Differences in presynaptic endocannabinoid signaling can account for the differential presence of DSI at CCK+ connections onto IT and PT cells.
source: These findings demonstrate that differences in presynaptic endocannabinoid signaling can account for the differential presence of DSI at CCK+ connections onto IT and PT cells.

claim: Depolarization of IT cells reduces vHPC-evoked IPSCs but not EPSCs at −50 mV (before, after, recovery: IPSC1 = 102 ± 14 pA, 51 ± 10 pA, 88 ± 10 pA; EPSC1 = 248 ± 54 pA, 233 ± 48 pA, 241 ± 52 pA; DSI ratio = 0.47 ± 0.05, p = 0.02; DSE ratio = 0.99 ± 0.06, p = 0.30).
source: Depolarization of IT cells (5 s to +10 mV) reduced vHPC-evoked IPSCs but not EPSCs at −50 mV (Figure 7B & E; before, after, recovery: IPSC1 = 102 ± 14 pA, 51 ± 10 pA, 88 ± 10 pA; EPSC1 = 248 ± 54 pA, 233 ± 48 pA, 241 ± 52 pA; DSI ratio = 0.47 ± 0.05, p = 0.02; DSE ratio = 0.99 ± 0.06, p = 0.30; n = 7 cells, 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by DSI experiments with vHPC stimulation shown in Figure 7B and E.

claim: There is no DSE at the vHPC to PFC connection, whereas there is prominent DSI onto IT cells.
source: These findings indicate that there is no DSE at the vHPC to PFC connection, whereas there is prominent DSI onto IT cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DSI/DSE data from Figure 7B and E.

claim: Application of AM-251 minimizes DSI of vHPC-evoked inhibition at IT cells (IPSC1: before = 136 ± 31 pA, after = 116 ± 29 pA, recovery = 149 ± 35 pA; DSI ratio = 0.84 ± 0.03, p = 0.02; DSI in ACSF versus AM-251, p = 0.0006).
source: Importantly, application of AM-251 minimized DSI, indicating that it is mediated by endocannabinoids activating CB1Rs (Figure 7C & E; IPSC1: before = 136 ± 31 pA, after = 116 ± 29 pA, recovery = 149 ± 35 pA; DSI ratio = 0.84 ± 0.03, p = 0.02; n = 7 cells, 3 animals; DSI in ACSF versus AM-251, p = 0.0006).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 7C and E.

claim: Depolarization of PT cells has minimal effect on either vHPC-evoked IPSCs or EPSCs (IPSC1before = 129 ± 32 pA, after = 114 ± 27 pA, recovery = 134 ± 33 pA; DSI ratio = 0.91 ± 0.05, p = 0.10; DSE ratio = 0.89 ± 0.04, p = 0.01).
source: In contrast, depolarization of PT cells had minimal effect on either vHPC-evoked IPSCs or EPSCs, confirming no DSI or DSE onto this postsynaptic cell type (Figure 7D & E; IPSC1before = 129 ± 32 pA, after = 114 ± 27 pA, recovery = 134 ± 33 pA; DSI ratio = 0.91 ± 0.05, p = 0.10; DSE ratio = 0.89 ± 0.04, p = 0.01; n = 10 cells, 4 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by DSI experiments with vHPC stimulation shown in Figure 7D and E.

source: These findings show that DSI of vHPC-evoked inhibition only occurs at IT cells, suggesting that CCK+ interneurons are a key node for activity-dependent modulation in communication between vHPC and PFC.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The abundance of CCK+ interneurons in the ventral mPFC is consistent with their role in cognitive and emotional behaviors.
source: The abundance of CCK+ interneurons in the ventral mPFC is consistent with their role in cognitive and emotional behaviors (Freund, 2003; Freund and Katona, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: vHPC inputs are strong and depressing onto CCK+ interneurons, in contrast to the facilitating inputs onto IT cells.
source: vHPC inputs are strong and depressing onto CCK+ interneurons, in contrast to the facilitating inputs onto IT cells (Liu and Carter, 2018).
evidence: This statement combines current findings with previous work by the authors.

claim: vHPC-evoked firing of CCK+ interneurons occurs without activation of IT cells, indicating polysynaptic recurrent activity is not required for activation of CCK+ interneurons.
source: Importantly, vHPC-evoked firing of CCK+ interneurons occurs without activation of IT cells, indicating polysynaptic recurrent activity is not required for activation of CCK+ interneurons, which are therefore likely to mediate feed-forward inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: In the hippocampus, CCK+ interneurons have been shown to participate in both feed-forward and feed-back networks.
source: Indeed, in the hippocampus, CCK+ interneurons have been shown to participate in both feed-forward and feed-back networks (Basu et al., 2013; Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

source: Our findings show that CCK+ interneurons have an important and underappreciated role in hippocampal evoked feed-forward inhibition, and it will be important to assess whether this generalizes to other inputs to the PFC.
evidence: This is a summary statement and speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The activation of PV+ interneurons by vHPC inputs is strong, consistent with their role in feed-forward inhibition in PFC and elsewhere.
source: The activation of PV+ interneurons is strong, consistent with their role in feed-forward inhibition in PFC and elsewhere (Anastasiades et al., 2018; Cruikshank et al., 2007; Delevich et al., 2015; Gabernet et al., 2005; McGarry and Carter, 2016).

source: Previous results have indicated that vHPC engages PV+ interneurons in superficial layers of the medial PFC (Marek et al., 2018).

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

source: SOM+ interneuron activation is weak, but increases with repetitive activity, similar to BLA inputs to superficial PFC (McGarry and Carter, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

source: The engagement of SOM+ interneurons is consistent with a role in oscillations linking the vHPC and PFC and involvement in working memory (Abbas et al., 2018).

source: Interestingly, the activation of SOM+ interneurons by long-range inputs also occurs in the granular sensory cortex, where it also builds during stimulus trains, suggesting this is a general property (Tan et al., 2008).

source: We found that CCK+ interneurons make robust inhibitory connections onto neighboring pyramidal cells in L5 of IL PFC.
evidence: This is a summary statement of findings from the manuscript.

source: Importantly, these connections are much stronger onto PT cells, similar to our previous findings for PV+, SOM+, and NDNF+ interneurons (Anastasiades et al., 2020; Anastasiades et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement combines current findings with previous work by the authors.

claim: Biased inhibition is a general property of inhibitory connections in the PFC, although strength also depends on intrinsic properties.
source: Biased inhibition is thus a general property of inhibitory connections in the PFC, although strength also depends on intrinsic properties (Anastasiades et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: In the hippocampus, CCK+ interneurons make unique connections onto different pyramidal cell populations defined by sublayer.
source: In the hippocampus, CCK+ interneurons also make unique connections onto different pyramidal cell populations defined by sublayer (Valero et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hippocampal CCK+ innervations vary along the somato-dendritic axis of pyramidal cells.
source: While hippocampal CCK+ innervations vary along the somato-dendritic axis of pyramidal cells (Bodor et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2010), our sCRACM results suggest CCK+ interneurons target the soma of both IT and PT cells in L5 of IL PFC.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The subcellular targeting of CCK+ interneurons to the soma could explain why there is little asynchronous CCK+ release.
source: This subcellular targeting could explain why we observed little asynchronous CCK+ release, which is stronger at dendritic synapses compared to somatic synapses at CCK+ connections in the hippocampus (Daw et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the sCRACM data and previous literature.

claim: IT and PT cells respond differently to many neuromodulators, including dopamine, acetylcholine, and serotonin, due to their distinct postsynaptic receptor expression profiles.
source: Due to their distinct postsynaptic receptor expression profiles, IT and PT cells are known to respond differently to many neuromodulators, including dopamine, acetylcholine, and serotonin (Anastasiades et al., 2019; Baker et al., 2018; Dembrow and Johnston, 2014; Shepherd, 2013; Stephens et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The endocannabinoid system shows marked cell-type specificity, with selective modulation on cortico-cortical networks.
source: Our result suggests the endocannabinoid system also shows marked cell-type specificity, with selective modulation on cortico-cortical networks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DSI data showing specificity for IT cells.

claim: The nanoscale organization of CB1Rs relative to voltage-gated calcium channels influences the effectiveness of presynaptic CB1Rs.
source: Previous studies indicate that the nanoscale organization of CB1Rs relative to voltage-gated calcium channels influences the effectiveness of presynaptic CB1Rs (Dudok et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The nanoscale organization of CB1Rs explains the weaker endocannabinoid modulation of dendritic-targeting than somatic-targeting CCK+ inputs in the hippocampus.
source: This explains the weaker endocannabinoid modulation of dendritic-targeting than somatic-targeting CCK+ inputs in the hippocampus (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Different nanoscale CB1R organizations could occur at boutons, making the CB1R at CCK+ inputs onto PT neurons non-functional.
source: Although we showed CCK+ interneurons restrict their targeting to the soma of both IT and PT cells, different nanoscale CB1R organizations could still occur at boutons, making the CB1R at CCK+ inputs onto PT neurons non-functional.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism for the observed cell-type specificity.

claim: Some PT-targeting CB1R+ boutons may come from other interneuron subtypes, as a small percentage of non-CCK+ cells also express CB1R.
source: Alternatively, some PT-targeting CB1R+ boutons may come from other interneuron subtypes, as previous studies showed that a small percentage of non-CCK+ cells also express CB1R (Bodor et al., 2005; Marsicano and Lutz, 1999).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several subtypes of CCK+ interneurons are found across the brain, which differ in their subcellular targeting of postsynaptic cells, the size of their soma, and the expression of molecular markers such as VIP and VGLUT3.
source: Indeed, several subtypes of CCK+ interneurons are found across the brain, which differ in their subcellular targeting of postsynaptic cells, the size of their soma, and the expression of molecular markers such as VIP and VGLUT3 (Bodor et al., 2005; del Pino et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2010; Omiya et al., 2015; Pelkey et al., 2020; Somogyi et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The ability of vHPC inputs to engage CCK+ interneurons, which in turn contact pyramidal cells, implicates a key role in feed-forward inhibition.
source: Ultimately, the ability of vHPC inputs to engage CCK+ interneurons, which in turn contact pyramidal cells, implicates a key role in feed-forward inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the connectivity data from the manuscript.

claim: CB1R-mediated DSI of vHPC-evoked inhibition only occurs at IT cells and not neighboring PT cells.
source: Consistent with this idea, we observed prominent CB1R-mediated DSI of vHPC-evoked inhibition only at IT cells and not neighboring PT cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement of findings from the manuscript.

claim: Because there is no change in excitation during DSI, this modulation will selectively increase the excitation/inhibition (E/I) ratio at IT cells.
source: Because there is no change in excitation, this modulation will selectively increase the excitation/inhibition (E/I) ratio at IT cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DSI data showing selective reduction of inhibition without change in excitation.

claim: When IT cells are highly active, increased endocannabinoid tone could promote local processing within the PFC.
source: In the intact brain, this could allow the vHPC to more effectively activate IT cells compared to neighboring PT cells. For example, when IT cells are highly active, increased endocannabinoid tone could promote local processing within the PFC.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications of the findings.

claim: Disinhibition at IT cells could allow for stronger responses to excitatory inputs, a potential mechanism for increased synchrony between hippocampus and PFC during working memory tasks and anxiety-like behavior.
source: Disinhibition at IT cells could also allow for stronger responses to excitatory inputs, a potential mechanism for increased synchrony between hippocampus and PFC during working memory tasks and anxiety-like behavior (Adhikari et al., 2010; Fujisawa and Buzsáki, 2011; O'Neill et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Altered E/I balance could potentially shift the output of the PFC toward other intratelencephalic targets throughout the brain, including other parts of the cortex, striatum, amygdala, and claustrum.
source: Furthermore, altered E/I balance could potentially shift the output of the PFC toward other intratelencephalic targets throughout the brain, including other parts of the cortex, striatum, amygdala, and claustrum (Anastasiades et al., 2019; Harris and Shepherd, 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Endocannabinoid signaling can strongly influence both cognition and emotion.
source: Previous studies have shown that endocannabinoid signaling can strongly influence both cognition and emotion (Mechoulam and Parker, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

source: Altering endocannabinoid levels also affects executive function, working memory, stress, anxiety, and threat learning (Lin et al., 2009; Lutz et al., 2015; Marcus et al., 2020; Marsicano et al., 2002; Volk and Lewis, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

source: Our results indicate endocannabinoids influence communication between vHPC to PFC by selectively modulating connections from CCK+ interneurons to IT cells.
